Methodology: Evidentiary Standards and Logical Rules

To judge fairly, the rules must be fixed before the evidence is examined and applied identically to both scriptures.

1. What counts as evidence

In descending order of weight:

  1. Physical manuscripts, dated by paleography and radiocarbon.
  2. Quotations and references in datable external sources (other authors, lectionaries, inscriptions, translations).
  3. The internal testimony of the tradition (how the community says its text was transmitted) — useful, but it is a claim about history, not automatically history.
  4. Apologetic argument — clarifies positions but is not evidence in itself.

2. Defining "corruption" precisely

The word corruption is used loosely in debate. This dossier distinguishes:

TypeDefinitionTest
Transmission corruptionThe text today differs materially from what was first writtenManuscript comparison across time
Compositional concernThe "original" itself is composite, anonymous, or lateSource criticism, dating
Interpretive corruption (tahrif al-maʿna)The wording is intact but meaning is distorted in readingExegetical, not textual
Wholesale fabricationThe text was invented and back-projectedExtraordinary claim; needs extraordinary evidence

A precise debate keeps these separate. Most apologetic confusion comes from sliding between them — e.g., citing trivial spelling variants (transmission) to argue the message was invented (fabrication).

3. The symmetry principle

Any argument is run in both directions:

  • "The Bible has hundreds of thousands of manuscript variants" → then the Qur'an's variant readings (qiraʾat) and the Sanaa palimpsest must be weighed by the same yardstick.
  • "The Qur'an was standardized by burning rival codices under ʿUthman" → then the church's selection and copying of the New Testament canon must be weighed by the same yardstick.

Selective skepticism — strict with the rival text, lenient with one's own — is the single most common fallacy in this field and is flagged wherever it appears.

4. Logical rules of engagement

  • The burden of proof lies on the claimant. "X is corrupt" requires evidence for corruption, not merely the absence of proof against it.
  • Quantity ≠ significance. 400,000 NT variants across 5,800+ Greek manuscripts is mostly an artifact of having many manuscripts; the metric that matters is whether variants change meaning or doctrine.
  • Absence of early manuscripts ≠ proof of change. It lowers certainty; it does not by itself prove corruption.
  • An argument that proves too much fails. A standard that declares the Bible "corrupt" but, applied evenly, would equally indict the Qur'an (or all ancient literature) is not a usable standard.
  • Genetic fallacy. A doctrine's late formalization (e.g., a creed ratified at a council) does not by itself prove the underlying idea was absent earlier — that must be shown from the sources.
  • Equivocation on "the Bible/Qur'an." Specify: Hebrew OT? Greek NT? Which textual tradition? Which qiraʾa? Vague nouns hide weak arguments.

5. Limits of the arbiter

History and textual criticism can answer what the text says and how it got here. They cannot answer whether its theology is true. When a section's question becomes "is God triune or absolutely one?", the arbiter rules only on (a) which view each scripture's own text better supports and (b) which view is internally coherent — not on which is divinely correct.
